title: Re-evaluation of xanthan gum (E 415) as a food additive in foods for infants below 16 weeks of age and follow-up of its re-evaluation as a food additive for uses in foods for all population groups
authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings (FAF), Younes M, Aquilina G, Castle L, Degen G, Engel KH, et al.
funder: European Food Safety Authority; requestor: European Commission; question number EFSA-Q-2018-00097.
result: For infants below 16 weeks of age fed special formulae for special medical purposes (food category 13.1.5.1), exposure at the maximum permitted level of 1,200 mg/L was estimated at 240 mg/kg body weight per day for mean and 312 mg/kg bw per day for high-level consumption, and at 183 and 238 mg/kg bw per day using the mean use levels reported by industry. The clinical studies submitted were of low validity and gave no reference point; the neonatal piglet studies gave a NOAEL of 750 mg/kg bw per day, and the resulting margin of exposure of 2.4 was considered sufficient because xanthan gum is not absorbed and an infant-specific animal model was used. Use in formulae for infants below 16 weeks up to 1,200 mg/L was concluded not to raise concerns. The Panel quoted the US Food and Drug Administration report of 22 infants who developed necrotising enterocolitis after use of a xanthan gum-containing thickener for gastro-oesophageal reflux or dysphagia: 21 were preterm with a median gestational age of 30.5 weeks, the thickener was consumed for a median of 13 days (range 1 to 31) before onset, 19 developed necrotising enterocolitis after 37 weeks post-menstrual age, 14 required surgery and 7 died; a further three extremely preterm infants were reported separately. In May 2011 the FDA warned parents and healthcare providers to avoid feeding the product to infants born before 37 weeks of gestation. The Panel judged that the described cases are not related to the food additive use of xanthan gum in the manufacture of infant formula and that the associated doses are unknown but expected in gram amounts, and noted that the opinion does not cover ad libitum addition of xanthan gum to mother's milk or infant formula. Xanthan gum forms a colloidal dispersion and will not be present in the gastrointestinal tract in the pristine particulate form, so a conventional risk assessment applies; the presence of small particles including nanoparticles could be neither confirmed nor excluded. Recommended amendments to the EU specifications include lowering the lead limit, adding limits for cadmium, mercury and arsenic, adding Cronobacter sakazakii to the microbiological criteria, requiring absence of residual enzyme activity and replacing 'soluble' with 'dispersible'. Highest quantified toxic element levels in commercial samples were lead 0.11, cadmium 0.01, mercury 0.007 and arsenic 0.1 mg/kg; with lead at the current specification limit of 2 mg/kg the margin of exposure for infants below 16 weeks at the 95th percentile was 0.8.
